Cart Before Horse

After each of our five team members picked a metric from the Fitbit data (heart rate for me), we did exploratory data analysis (EDA) separately, then each used the Crazy 8 method to generate 40 User Requirements (URs). I now think this was premature, and we should have fleshed out our project idea before doing URs. Many of them are vague or have little relevance to the finished dashboard. However, it was a fun exercise and would have been effective if timed more strategically.

Shiny

In a group discussion about which software to use for the dashboard, Abdi and I volunteered to use R Shiny, which neither of us had used. R is the language of choice at the ONS, where we both work, so we were both keen to learn the package. We arranged a Teams session and worked through Posit’s official Shiny tutorials. I find collaborative coding sessions to be excellent for motivation compared to endless solo learning on platforms like DataCamp.

EDA

My favourite analysis involved looking at 24 hours’ worth of standardised heart rate data for one individual and applying a K-Means model, which uses machine learning to look for patterns in the data and divide it into a given number of clusters.

I had ambitious ideas for a K-Means dashboard for each of our metrics—something along these lines—but when I pitched it to the team they (quite rightly) advised aiming smaller for our MVP, and we settled on the Awards concept, using four metrics from our EDA to find the standout individual for each metric.

Dashboard Build and Git

I was pleased with the project structure, which we divided into a data prep and an app-launching script.

However, our GitHub repo could have been better organised, with more clarity on when to merge and when to branch, etc.

Closing Thoughts

The biggest lesson learnt has been the importance of settling on a team structure. Now that one man and his AI can independently see a project through, a siloed team structure is harder to make work. For future group projects, a flat team structure with plenty of co-coding sessions might be the way to go.

I had this in mind writing this reflection, but working on the app and video reinforced the idea that AI, when used smartly and selectively, can lead to distinctive output—not the homogenous plastic sheen of PowerPoint slop.
